content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method to synthesize anomaly samples by learning a noise to be added to normal samples with a generative model (autoencoder structure). The synthesized anomalies are used with normal samples to train an autoencoder (AE) based anomaly detector (AD). AD learns to reconstruct normal samples while forced to fail the reconstruction of pseudo anomalies. By doing so, the learned AD alleviates the problem of reconstructing anomalies which is a well-known problem of AE-based AD approaches. The proposed method is validated on three video datasets and one image dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

### The motivation is clear and important.

AE-based models are dominating approaches in image/video-based anomaly detection.
However, AE is likely to reconstruct outliers as well which is a known problem for AD tasks.
One solution is to use synthetic anomalies in training; however, generation or augmentation methods require domain knowledge and vary across different modalities.
The learnable way proposed in this paper is domain and modality agnostic which applies to a wide range of applications.

### Simple and straightforward approach.

The algorithm is not complicated and although two hyperparameters are introduced, lambda and p, these are hyperparameters commonly used in most learning methods to balance multiple loss terms.



## Weakness

### The experiments are only performed on image datasets.

The one main strength and motivation of the paper is that anomalies can be learned from data without strong assumptions which make it domain- and modality-agnostic.
However, most of the experiments are performed on image domains.
The paper should experiment with NLP and tabular datasets to validate its general applicability in other modalities.
Some of the datasets commonly used other than image datasets are KDD cup (or KDD-rev) [1], Reuter [2], or PyOD benchmarks [3].

[1] http://kdd.ics.uci.edu/databases/kddcup99/kddcup99.html

[2] https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/reuters-21578+text+categorization+collection

[3] https://pyod.readthedocs.io/en/latest/benchmark.html

### Missing related work

The previous work [1] also tackles the same problem but not discussed nor compared in the experiments.

[1] Yoon, Sangwoong, Yung-Kyun Noh, and Frank Park. "Autoencoding under normalization constraints." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.



### It is unclear whether the experiments are repeated multiple times and averaged, or only reporting the best performance.

The ablation study in figure6 is repeated 5 times, then average and best performances are reported. But there is no description of the number of experiments repeated in table 1. Also, standard deviation is not reported.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

- In section2 ‘Adversarial training’ paragraph, the sentence
‘Moreover, instead of aiming to generate real-looking data, our method attempts to generate data that is highly noisy but at the same time not impossible for the AE to reconstruct’
The sentence is confusing because the goal of the method is to make AE fail to reconstruct pseudo anomalies. But this sentence says pseudo anomalies should be able to be reconstructed, or not impossible to reconstruct by AE. This should be clarified.

- Equation (3) is designed for AE to fail the reconstruction of pseudo anomalies. However, this is not described explicitly anywhere in the paper. Without explicit description, it looks like the AE is reconstructing both pseudo anomalies and normal samples with recon loss. Re-addressing the role of equation (3) would clarify readers to understand the paper easily.

- In the caption of table 1, what does ‘generic method’ mean?

- Table 1 lists a lot of methods. It will be easier if the methods can be grouped into categories, for example, the ones using strong assumptions and ones that are not.

- show standard deviation as a colored region in the graph of figure 6.


### Quality

The paper is understandable overall, although minor polishing would improve the paper.

### Novelty

The paper tackles domain/modality-agnostic pseudo anomaly generation which is an important and interesting topic.

### Reproducibility

The code is not provided. But most of the implementation details are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper tackles an important problem and the approach is not complicated. However, the paper did not thoroughly verify the important aspect of the method which is modality-agnostic.
A minor improvement of the manuscript is also recommended.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The work introduces a method to produce learnable noises as pseudo anomalies for improving the detection performance of autoencoder (AE)-based anomaly detection methods. The main objective is to eliminate the dependence on the use of inductive bias in the pseudo anomaly generation as done in related work. To this end, an additional AE is used as the noise data generator, and it is alternatively trained with the anomaly detection AE. The method is evaluated on three video anomaly detection datasets and one image dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The work has the following strengths.
- The idea of generating learnable noises in assisting the generation of pseudo anomalies is new, and it is a good way to eliminate the dependence on the use of inductive bias in the pseudo anomaly generation as done in related work. 
- The two-AE framework to implement the idea is reasonable.
- The graphical illustrations are good and well support the understanding of the intuitions behind the idea.
- The empirical results on three video anomaly detection datasets and one image dataset show that the method improves over the simple baseline and Gaussian noise-based pseudo anomaly generation methods.

The work also has a number of major issues.
- It is difficult to understand why minimizing eq. 2 would result in a mode that well-reconstructs normal data and poorly-reconstructs pseudo anomalous data.
- Generating pseudo anomalies in the original feature space is good, but it is unclear what advantages this approach has compared to those that generate the anomalies in the low-dimensional latent space, such as the studies mentioned in "Generation of Out-of-Distribution Data". My understanding is the latter is more plausible as the former faces much greater challenges. Actually, the demonstration in Figure 4 shows a similar resulting latent space as the ones obtained by the latter approaches. Discussions on the pros and cons from this aspect are required. Empirical comparisons are also required to support the pros of the method. 
- Although the pseudo anomalies are learnable, the method significantly underperforms the methods that use simple data augmentation to generate the pseudo anomalies, such as those compared in Table 1. This shows ineffective performance of the method compared to closely relevant methods. Further, the improvement over the simple baseline and the Gaussian noise-based baselines is very marginal. These results show that the proposed method does not make much contribution even compared to simple baselines.
- The method is also far below the results of current SOTA, as shown in Table 7.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper clarity is generally good. The idea is fairly new, but there are many alternative (simpler) solutions.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the work makes a good attempt to improve AE-based anomaly detection approaches, but the method does not have major contributions to relevant lines of research.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors study the task of anomaly detection in videos, presenting an auto-encoder model based on learning not to reconstruct pseudo-anomalies. The pseudo-anomalies are constructed via two options: a) adding random Gaussian noise to normal samples, or b) adding a learned noise to normal samples. The method is evaluated on three datasets (Avenue, ShanghaiTech, UCSD Ped2), being compared with some baselines from the literature.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper addresses an important and timely topic.
- The paper is generally easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
- The proposed idea seems like a minor modification of denoising auto-encoders. Moreover, pseudo-anomalies have been using in different previous papers. The only contribution is the idea of “learnable noise”, but this idea leads to minor performance improvements compared to random Gaussian noise. Hence, I believe the proposed method exhibits very little novelty.
- The proposed method does not compare with recent state-of-the-art reconstruction methods, e.g. SSPCAB [A]. Moreover, many other state-of-the-art peer-reviewed methods listed in public rankings [B, C] are missed by the authors. The results reported by the authors are quite far from the top results, being about 10% lower on Avenue and ShanghaiTech.
- An important feature of anomaly detection methods is the inference time, which is expected to be real-time. Unfortunately, the running time of the proposed method is not discussed by the authors. 
- The idea of using pseudo-anomalies and learning not to reconstruct them (via adversarial training) has also been proposed in (Georgescu et al, 2021). This work should be placed in the correct category of methods by the authors.
- Ramachandra et al. [E] recommends using the RBDC / TBDC as more relevant measures for anomaly detection. The authors should include these measures in their evaluation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper and contribution are clear, yet the novelty is low.
content.summary_of_the_review: In my opinion, the work has some major drawbacks (listed in the weaknesses section) which prevented me from taking a more positive decision.

content.title: Learning to Generate Pseudo Anomalies
content.TL;DR: We propose learning mechanism to generate pseudo anomalies for one-class classification in anomaly detection.
content.abstract: Due to rare occurrence of anomalous events, anomaly detection is often seen as one-class classification (OCC) problem. In this setting, an autoencoder (AE) is typically trained to reconstruct using only normal data in order to learn normalcy representations. It is expected that, at test time, the AE can well reconstruct normal data while poorly reconstructing anomalous data. However, anomalous data is often well reconstructed as well. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that when training AE with only normal data, the boundary between normal and abnormal data is unknown, consequently resulting in a boundary that includes the abnormal data as well. To alleviate this problem, we utilize pseudo anomalies to limit the reconstruction capability of an AE. Without imposing strong inductive bias, pseudo anomalies are generated by adding noise to the normal data. Moreover, to improve the quality of pseudo anomalies, we propose a learning mechanism to generate noise by exploiting the aforementioned weakness of AE, i.e., reconstructing anomalies too well. Evaluations on Ped2, Avenue, ShanghaiTech, and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving the discriminative capability of AEs for anomaly detection.
